passages.source_text: ὅτι δὲ πρὸς τὰς προλήψεις ἡ ἑκάστου ψυχὴ ἰδέας δαιμόνων ἀπεικονίζει καὶ οὐχ οἱ λεγόμενοι θεοὶ ἐπιφαίνονται, σαφές ἐστιν ἐκ τοῦ Ἰουδαίοις μὴ ἐπιφαίνεσθαι. ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις Πῶς οὖν χρηματίζουσιν τὰ μέλλοντα προσημαίνοντες; καὶ τοῦτο ψεῦδός ἐστιν. δεδόσθω δὲ ἀλήθειαν εἶναι, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν. οὐ γὰρ εἴ τι μαντεύεται, θεός ἐστιν· ὅτι καὶ πύθωνες μαντεύονται, ἀλλ’ ὑφ’ ἡμῶν ὡς δαίμονες ὁρκιζόμενοι φυγαδεύονται. ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις Ἐνίοις θεραπείας προστάσσουσιν. ψεῦδός ἐστιν· δεδόσθω δὲ οὕτως ἔχειν, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν. καὶ γὰρ ἰατροὶ ἰῶνται πολλοὺς καὶ θεοὶ οὐκ εἰσίν. ἀλλὰ (φησίν) ἰατροὶ οὐ πάντως ἰῶνται ἐκείνους, ὧν τὴν πρόνοιαν ποιοῦνται, οὗτοι δὲ καὶ χρηματίσαντες ἰῶνται. ἀλλ’ ἴσασιν οἱ δαίμονες τὰ ὄντως πρὸς ἕκαστον πάθος προσῳκειωμένα βοηθήματα· διὸ ἰατροὶ ἐπιστήμονες ἰᾶσθαι δυνάμενοι, καὶ ταῦτα τὰ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων ἰαθῆναι δυνάμενα, ἀλλὰ καὶ μαντικὰ ὄντα καὶ εἰδότα πότε ἕκαστον ἐξ αὐτομάτου θεραπεύεται, τότε συντάσσουσιν τὰς θεραπείας, ἵνα ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιγράψωσιν.

ἐπεὶ διὰ τί μετὰ πολὺν χρόνον χρηματίζουσιν τὰς ἰάσεις; διὰ τί δέ, εἰ πάντα δύνανται, ἄνευ τοῦ προσφέρειν τι τὴν ἴασιν οὐ ποιοῦνται; τίνος δὲ ἕνεκα τισὶν μὲν εὐξαμένοις θεραπείας προστάσσουσιν, ἐνίοις δὲ ἔσθ’ ὅτε καὶ οἰκειοτέροις οὖσιν οὐ χρηματίζουσιν; οὕτως ὁπόταν ἐξ αὐτομάτου θεραπεία μέλλῃ γίνεσθαι, ἐπαγγέλλονται, ἵνα ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιγράψωσιν. ἄλλοι δὲ νοσήσαντες καὶ εὐξάμενοι ἐξ αὐτομάτου ὑγιάναντες, οὓς ἐπεκαλέσαντο ἐπέγραψαν καὶ ἀναθήματα ἐποίησαν. οἱ μέντοι γε μετὰ εὐχὴν διαφωνήσαντες τὰς ἀποτυχίας ἀναθεῖναι οὐ δύνανται. πλὴν εἰ οἱ συγγενεῖς τῶν τεθνεώτων ἢ ἐξ αὐτῶν τινὲς συνεζήτησαν τὰς ἀποτυχίας, πλείονας ἂν εὑρήκειτε τὰς ἀποτυχίας τῶν ἐπιτευγμάτων. ἀλλ’ οὐδεὶς προειλημμένος αὐτοῖς τὸν κατ’ αὐτῶν, ἔλεγχον ἐκφᾶναι θέλει αἰδούμενος ἢ φοβούμενος, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον τὰ πιστὰ αὐτῶν ἀτοπήματα συνκρύβουσιν.

πόσοι δὲ καὶ καταψεύδονται χρηματισμοὺς καὶ θεραπείας ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀποτελεσθείσας καὶ ταύτας βεβαιοῦνται μετὰ ὅρκων; πόσοι δὲ ἐπὶ μισθῷ ἑαυτοὺς ἐξέδωκαν, δι’ ἐνίων ἐπινοιῶν πάσχειν τινὰ ἀναδεξάμενοι καὶ οὕτως κηρύξαντες, αὐτῶν τὸ πάθος ἀντιπαθείᾳ ἀποκατασταθέντες, κεχρηματίσθαι τὴν θεραπείαν λέγουσιν, ἵνα τὸ ἀναίσθητον ἐπιγράψωσιν σέβασμα; πόσα δὲ αὐτῶν ἐκ καταρχῆς μαγικῇ τέχνῃ ἐτελέσθη, ἵνα ὑνερπολῇ καὶ χρηματίζῃ; καὶ ὅμως μακρῷ χρόνῳ καὶ ταῦτα διεφώνησεν. πόσοι δὲ νῦν τὰ τοιαῦτα κρατύνειν θέλοντες γοητεύουσιν; πλὴν οὐκ εἴ τι μαντικόν ἐστιν ἢ θεραπευτικόν, τοῦτο θεός ἐστιν.

ὁ γὰρ θεὸς πάντα δύναται. ἐκεῖνος γάρ ἐστιν ἀγαθὸς καὶ δίκαιος, νῦν πᾶσιν μακροθυμῶν, ἵνα οἱ βουλόμενοι ἐφ’ οἷς ἔπραξαν κακοῖς μεταμεληθέντες καὶ πολιτευσάμενοι, ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ᾗ τὰ πάντα κρίνεται, κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπολαύσωσιν. διὸ νῦν ἄρξασθε, ἀγαθῆς γνώσεως αἰτίᾳ θεῷ πειθόμενοι ἀντιλέγειν ὑμῶν ταῖς κακαῖς ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἐννοίαις, ἵνα δυνηθῆτε ἀνακαλέσασθαι τὴν πρώτην τῇ ἀνθρωπότητι παραδοθεῖσαν σωτήριον θρησκείαν. οὕτω γὰρ ὑμῖν ἐξαυτῆς ἀνατελεῖ τὰ ἀγαθά, ἅτινα λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν τοῦ λοιποῦ καταλείψετε. ἀλλὰ τῷ δεδωκότι εὐχαριστήσατε, μετὰ τοῦ τῆς εἰρήνης βασιλέως εἰσαεὶ τῶν ἀπορρήτων βασιλεύοντες ἀγαθῶν. ἐν δὲ τῷ παρόντι, ἀενάῳ ποταμῷ ἢ πηγῇ ἐπεί γε κἂν θαλάσσῃ ἀπολουσάμενοι ἐπὶ τῇ τρισμακαρίᾳ ἐπονομασίᾳ οὐ μόνον τὰ ἐνδομυχοῦντα ὑμῖν πνεύματα ἀπελάσαι δυνήσεσθε, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοὶ μηκέτι ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ θεῷ ἀνενδοιάστως πιστεύοντες τὰ ἄλλων κακὰ πνεύματα καὶ δαιμόνια χαλεπὰ σὺν τοῖς δεινοῖς πάθεσιν ἀπελάσετε. ἐνίοτε δὲ μόνον ἐνδόντων ὑμῶν φεύξονται· ἴσασιν γὰρ τοὺς ἀποδεδωκότας ἑαυτοὺς τῷ θεῷ, διὸ τιμῶντες αὐτοὺς πεφοβημένοι φεύγουσιν, ὥσπερ ἐχθὲς ἑωράκατε πῶς ἐμοῦ ἀναθεμένου μετὰ τὴν προσομιλίαν εὔξασθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν πασχόντων αὐτὰ τὰ πάθη τῇ πρὸς τὴν θρησκείαν τιμῇ ἀνέκραγεν, βραχεῖαν ὥραν στέξαι μὴ δυνηθέντα.

μὴ οὖν νομίσητε ὅτι ἡμεῖς ἄλλης φύσεως ὄντες κατὰ τοῦτο δαίμονας οὐ φοβούμεθα. τῆς γὰρ αὐτῆς ὑμῖν ἐσμὲν φύσεως, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ θρησκείας. διὸ ὑμῶν οὐ πολύ, ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν κρείττονες ὄντες καὶ ὑμᾶς τοιούτους γενέσθαι οὐ φθονοῦμεν, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον συμβουλεύομεν, εἰδότες ὅτι τοὺς θεῷ προσοικειωθέντας ταῦτα πάντα ἀγνώστως προτιμᾷ καὶ φοβεῖται.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: That each person’s soul, in accordance with its preconceptions, portrays forms of demons, and that the so-called gods do not appear, is clear from the fact that they do not appear to Jews. But someone will say, “How, then, do they deliver oracles that foretell the future?” This too is false. Yet grant that it is true: does that make such a thing a god? For something is not a god merely because it foretells the future. Python mediums also foretell the future, but when we adjure them as demons, they are driven away. But someone will say, “They prescribe treatments for some people.” That is false. Yet grant that this is so: does that make such a thing a god? Physicians also heal many people, and they are not gods. “But,” someone says, “physicians do not invariably heal those for whom they care, whereas these both deliver an oracle and heal.” Demons, however, know the remedies truly suited to each particular ailment. Consequently, they are knowledgeable physicians, capable of healing—and that in cases capable of being healed by human beings. But they are also divinatory beings and know when each person will recover spontaneously; at that moment they prescribe the treatments, so that they may claim the credit for themselves.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in accordance with its preconceptions
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός with the accusative here indicates correspondence to each soul’s prior conceptions, which determine the forms it portrays.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Python mediums
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes persons or agencies associated with a Python spirit and practicing divination; alternatives include “Python spirits” and “those possessed by Python.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δεδόσθω δὲ ἀλήθειαν εἶναι, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet grant that it is true: does that make such a thing a god?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although the final clause can be punctuated as a statement, the following denial shows that it functions rhetorically: even genuine prediction would not establish divinity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ταῦτα τὰ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων ἰαθῆναι δυνάμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: and that in cases capable of being healed by human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The emphatic καὶ ταῦτα limits or qualifies the preceding ability: the ailments in question are also within the scope of human medicine. A more literal alternative is “and these being things capable of being healed by humans.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they may claim the credit for themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, they seek to “inscribe” themselves upon the cure, idiomatically attaching their own name or credit to it.

source_issues.issue: The printed text shifts to neuter plural participial forms after the masculine subjects οἱ δαίμονες and ἰατροὶ ... δυνάμενοι. This may be an anacoluthon or may imply the neuter δαιμόνια. English can preserve the demons as the semantic subject without resolving the morphological shift.

passages.text: For why do they announce healings by oracle only after a long time? Why, if they can do everything, do they not bring about healing without an offering? Why do they prescribe treatments for some who pray, but sometimes deliver no oracle to others who are even more closely connected with them? It is in this way: whenever a spontaneous recovery is about to occur, they make a promise so that they may claim the credit for themselves. Others fell ill and prayed, and when they recovered spontaneously, they credited those whom they had invoked and made votive offerings. Those, however, for whom matters turned out otherwise after prayer cannot dedicate their failures. Yet if the relatives of the dead, or some of those people themselves, were to compile the failures, you would find the failures more numerous than the successes. But no one who is already prepossessed in their favor wants to expose the case against them, being ashamed or afraid. On the contrary, they join in concealing their well-attested absurdities.

lexical_decisions.chosen: without an offering
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized infinitive refers to presenting something, naturally an offering in this cultic context; “without presenting anything” is the more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who are even more closely connected with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative describes a closer relationship or affiliation, though whether familial, cultic, or generally intimate is not specified.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ μέντοι γε μετὰ εὐχὴν διαφωνήσαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: Those, however, for whom matters turned out otherwise after prayer
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφωνέω literally concerns disagreement or discrepancy; here it contrasts unsuccessful outcomes with the reported recoveries.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were to compile the failures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean investigate or examine together; “compile” fits the comparison between the total numbers of failures and successes. “Jointly investigate the failures” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: already prepossessed in their favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle describes someone whose judgment has already been captured or prejudiced by them; “previously taken in by them” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their well-attested absurdities
lexical_decisions.rationale: πιστά can mean trustworthy, credible, or firmly established. Here it characterizes the ἀτοπήματα as reliable evidence of their absurd conduct, not as conduct worthy of trust.

source_issues.issue: The print has the unassimilated compound spelling συνκρύβουσιν where συγκρύβουσιν would be the standard assimilated form. The sense “conceal together” or “join in concealing” remains clear.

passages.text: How many also falsely claim that oracles were given and that healings were accomplished by them, and confirm these claims with oaths? How many have hired themselves out for pay, undertaking through various contrivances to suffer some ailment and advertising it as such; then, after being restored from their ailment by counteraction, they say that the treatment had been prescribed by oracle, so that they may credit the insensible object of worship? How many of them were established from the outset by magical art, so that it might ὑνερπολῇ and deliver oracles? And yet, after a long time, these too failed. How many now practice sorcery because they want to strengthen such things? Nevertheless, something is not a god merely because it can foretell the future or bring healing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have hired themselves out for pay
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression describes placing oneself at another’s disposal in return for payment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δι’ ἐνίων ἐπινοιῶν πάσχειν τινὰ ἀναδεξάμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: undertaking through various contrivances to suffer some ailment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίνοιαι are devised schemes or contrivances, while ἀναδέχομαι indicates undertaking or assuming the staged affliction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after being restored from their ailment by counteraction
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀντιπάθεια denotes an opposing or counteracting influence, possibly a treatment by contraries; the source does not specify its mechanism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they may credit the insensible object of worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: As in 9.16, ἐπιγράφω concerns attaching a name or credit. The object of worship is characterized as without perception or sensation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: How many of them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural may refer to the objects of worship just mentioned or more generally to such cultic phenomena; the English leaves the referent open.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὅμως μακρῷ χρόνῳ καὶ ταῦτα διεφώνησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: And yet, after a long time, these too failed
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφωνέω here indicates that the promised or manufactured results ceased to agree with the claims and proved unsuccessful; “turned out otherwise” is an alternative.

source_issues.issue: The image-checked print clearly reads ὑνερπολῇ, but no defensible lexical sense or regular formation can be established for that supplied form. It has therefore been retained untranslated rather than silently replaced. The conjecture ὑπερπολῇ could mean “gain ascendancy” or “flourish,” but that wording is not the selected edition’s reading and has not been imported into the translation.

passages.text: For God can do everything. He is good and just, showing patience toward everyone now, so that those who are willing may regret the evils they have committed and live accordingly, and, on the day when everything is judged, receive what they deserve. Therefore begin now, obeying God, the cause of good knowledge, to oppose your evil desires and thoughts, so that you may recover for yourselves the original saving religion handed down to humanity. In this way good things will immediately spring up for you; once you have received them, you will thereafter leave behind your experience of evils. But give thanks to the one who gave them, reigning forever with the King of Peace over the inexpressible good things. In the present, after washing yourselves in an ever-flowing river or spring, or indeed even in the sea, with the thrice-blessed invocation, you will be able not only to drive away the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses, but also—if you yourselves no longer sin and believe God without wavering—to drive out other people’s evil spirits and fierce demons, together with their dreadful afflictions. Sometimes, however, they will flee when you merely yield. For they recognize those who have given themselves to God, and therefore, showing them honor, they flee in fear. Just yesterday you saw how, when after the discourse I undertook to pray for those who were suffering, the afflictions themselves cried aloud out of respect for the religion, unable to endure even a short time.

lexical_decisions.chosen: may regret
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes regret or a change of concern regarding the evils committed. It is kept distinct from the μετανοέω terminology governed by the reorientation policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and live accordingly
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεύομαι concerns conducting one’s life. “Accordingly” expresses the contextual connection with regret without adding a new intensifier; “conduct their lives” is the more formally literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: obeying God, the cause of good knowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative αἰτίᾳ can stand in apposition to θεῷ, identifying God as the cause of good knowledge. Another possible attachment is “for the sake of good knowledge, obeying God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πρώτην τῇ ἀνθρωπότητι παραδοθεῖσαν σωτήριον θρησκείαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the original saving religion handed down to humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρώτην characterizes the religion as first or original, while σωτήριον describes it as saving. The wording preserves the author’s historical claim without harmonization.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν τοῦ λοιποῦ καταλείψετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: once you have received them, you will thereafter leave behind your experience of evils
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἅτινα is taken as the object of λαβόντες, while πεῖραν is the object of καταλείψετε and τῶν κακῶν depends on πεῖραν. This avoids changing the case relationships.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the thrice-blessed invocation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπονομασία can mean naming, designation, or invocation. In the washing context, “invocation” best conveys an enacted naming formula without supplying its unquoted words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδομυχέω depicts dwelling or hiding deep within, preserving the spatial image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when you merely yield
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive absolute uses ἐνδίδωμι in its intransitive sense “yield” or “give way.” In context this may mean yielding oneself to God, as the following clause explains; “when you merely permit it” is another possible sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the afflictions themselves cried aloud
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb, a normal Greek construction. The personification or identification of the afflictions with their spiritual agents is preserved rather than explained away.

passages.text: Therefore, do not suppose that because we are of another nature, we do not fear demons. For we are of the same nature as you, though not of the same religion. Consequently, although we are not merely a little but altogether superior to you, we do not begrudge your becoming the same; on the contrary, we recommend it, knowing that all these beings, without understanding, esteem and fear those who have become closely allied with God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς γὰρ αὐτῆς ὑμῖν ἐσμὲν φύσεως, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ θρησκείας
lexical_decisions.chosen: For we are of the same nature as you, though not of the same religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The second genitive is elliptical, contrasting shared human nature with differing religion or worship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ πολύ, ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν κρείττονες
lexical_decisions.chosen: not merely a little but altogether superior
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast emphatically denies a small degree of superiority and asserts it comprehensively; “superior in every respect” is a possible stronger English formulation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὑμᾶς τοιούτους γενέσθαι οὐ φθονοῦμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we do not begrudge your becoming the same
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοιούτους refers to becoming people of the same religious standing just described, while φθονέω means begrudge or envy another’s acquisition of it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have become closely allied with God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσοικειόω denotes being brought into close relationship or affinity. Alternatives include “those made God’s own” and “those who have drawn near to God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταῦτα πάντα ἀγνώστως προτιμᾷ καὶ φοβεῖται
lexical_decisions.chosen: all these beings, without understanding, esteem and fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural collectively refers to the demonic beings under discussion and therefore takes singular Greek verbs. ἀγνώστως may mean “unknowingly,” “without understanding,” or “in an inexplicable manner”; the chosen wording allows them to recognize God’s people, as stated previously, without necessarily understanding the reason for their authority.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
